title: COP31 ends without a deal after EU rejects fossil fuel text
h1: The COP31 climate summit in Turkey ended without a final agreement after the European Union rejected a text that left out fossil fuels
description: COP31 in Antalya, Turkey ended November 22, 2026 with no final agreement after the EU rejected a draft that did not mention fossil fuels. Here is what failed.
standfirst: The talks ran two days over and became the longest U.N. climate conference on record. Pledges on electrification and adaptation funding fell with the main decision.
keywords: COP31, Antalya climate summit, COP31 no agreement, fossil fuels climate talks, European Union walkout, Wopke Hoekstra, climate finance 2026
takeaways: COP31 ended on November 22, 2026 in Antalya, Turkey, with no overall agreement among nearly 200 countries.
The EU refused any text that did not mention fossil fuels; oil producers including Saudi Arabia opposed that language.
A pledge to raise global electrification to 35% by 2035 failed along with the main decision.
body: The United Nations climate summit known as COP31 ended on Sunday, November 22, in Antalya, Turkey, without a final agreement. Delegates from nearly 200 countries could not settle a dispute over whether the text should address fossil fuels, NPR reported. The talks ran two days past their scheduled end and became the longest conference in the history of the summits.

The European Union refused to accept an outcome that did not call for a transition away from fossil fuels, while oil-producing countries such as Saudi Arabia opposed that language. Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, and EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra left the room, according to NPR. Panama, Belize, Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands also objected to the text.

U.N. climate conferences work by consensus, so one country's objection can block a deal. COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, said the draft was not adopted because parties in the hall opposed it, CBS News reported. An early draft had called for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, but that wording was removed within days, according to CBS.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed" by the outcome, CBS reported.

Organizers had billed the meeting as a summit on electrification. Dozens of countries signed a pledge to raise electricity's share of global energy use from about 23% to 35% by 2035, but it did not pass once the main decision failed, NPR reported. Measures meant to deliver on tripling adaptation funding for vulnerable countries by 2035 were part of the same rejected decision.
New pledges to help countries with climate damages came to $142 million at the summit, which NPR described as far less than at other recent conferences.
The United States sent no delegation for the second year in a row, both outlets reported.

More than 50 countries have started a separate conference process on phasing out fossil fuels, and Ireland and Tuvalu will co-host its second meeting in 2027, according to NPR. Australian minister Chris Bowen, who ran the negotiations, told reporters afterward that the shift away from fossil fuels is already under way outside the U.N. process.
